claims.claim: Cancer cells respond to CIN with IL6-STAT3 signaling that protects from CIN-induced cell death.
claims.source: MPS1i-treated cancer cells have also been reported to escape immune-mediated clearance (Wang et al., 2021), with another study reporting that cancer cells respond to CIN with IL6-STAT3 signaling (Hong et al., 2022) that protects from CIN-induced cell death, allows cells to adapt to CIN- and aneuploidy-induced stresses, and minimizes interferon-related anti-cancer responses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study.

claims.claim: Ploidy changes tend to increase factors that can promote macrophage-mediated phagocytosis.
claims.source: On the other hand, ploidy changes tend to increase factors that can promote macrophage-mediated phagocytosis (Chao et al., 2010; Krysko et al., 2018), which led us to hypothesize that macrophages can be manipulated to more productively counter CIN- and aneuploidy-afflicted tumors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claims.claim: Phagocytosis of 'self' cells including cancer cells is generally inhibited by the macrophage checkpoint interaction between SIRPα on the macrophage and ubiquitously expressed CD47 on any target cell.
claims.source: Phagocytosis of 'self' cells including cancer cells is generally inhibited by the macrophage checkpoint interaction between SIRPα on the macrophage and ubiquitously expressed CD47 on any target cell (Oldenborg et al., 2000; Tsai and Discher, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claims.claim: Maximal macrophage-mediated phagocytosis is achieved when CD47-SIRPα signaling is simultaneously disrupted.
claims.source: Maximal macrophage-mediated phagocytosis is achieved when CD47-SIRPα signaling is simultaneously disrupted.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the CD47-SIRPα checkpoint.

claims.claim: Multiple clinical trials of antibody blockade of CD47 have been stopped due to safety concerns and little to no efficacy.
claims.source: In patients, multiple clinical trials of antibody blockade of CD47 have been stopped due to safety concerns and little to no efficacy - which motivates more fundamental studies as well as safer approaches.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of clinical trial outcomes.

claims.claim: CIN and ploidy changes inhibit tumor growth in immunocompetent mice while having little effect in immunocompromised mice.
claims.source: CIN and ploidy changes also inhibit tumor growth in immunocompetent mice while having little effect in immunocompromised mice (Senovilla et al., 2012; Boilève et al., 2013), which suggests CIN somehow increases immunogenicity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claims.claim: Early-stage CIN induces a senescence-associated secretory pathway phenotype and upregulation of NF-κB and interferon-mediated pathways.
claims.source: CIN in diploid cells that is caused by spindle assembly checkpoint disruption via MPS1 kinase inhibition (MPS1i) further induces a senescence-associated secretory pathway phenotype and upregulation of NF-κB and interferon-mediated pathways, among others, that drive immune clearance of chromosomally aberrant cells (Santaguida et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cited previous studies.

claims.claim: B16F10 tumors are poorly immunogenic and do not respond to either anti-CD47 or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapies.
claims.source: The result is notable given that B16F10 tumors are poorly immunogenic, do not respond to either anti-CD47 or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapies, and show modest and variable cure rates (~20–40%; Dooling et al., 2023; Hayes et al., 2023) even when macrophages have been made maximally phagocytic according to notions above.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about B16F10 tumors and is consistent with cited previous studies.

results.result: MPS1 inhibitor treatment induces chromosomal instability (CIN) in B16F10 melanoma cells, as evidenced by >10-fold increase in micronuclei that persist for up to 12 days and result in 34% of cells showing aneuploidy by InferCNV analysis compared to 10% in controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 provide converging evidence from multiple assays (microscopy, time-course, and single-cell RNA-seq with InferCNV) that MPS1i treatment successfully induces CIN. The quantitative data are consistent across methods and confirmed with multiple inhibitors (C1), demonstrating robust induction of chromosomal instability.

results.result: CIN-afflicted tumors show transcriptional downregulation of M2-like pro-cancer macrophage markers and associated cytokines at days 5 and 10 post-challenge, along with downregulation of DNA damage, cell cycle, and growth pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 are supported by bulk RNA-sequencing data from whole tumors at two timepoints (Figure 1E-F). The findings are internally consistent and align with cited literature. However, the study uses only n=2 tumors per condition, which limits statistical power. Despite this limitation, the consistency across timepoints and pathway analyses supports the conclusions.

results.result: Conditioned media from MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells polarizes bone marrow-derived macrophages toward an M1-like anti-cancer phenotype with increased pro-inflammatory markers and decreased M2-like markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing of BMDMs treated with conditioned media (Figure 1I-J). The clustering analysis clearly separates macrophages by treatment condition, and marker expression patterns are consistent with M1 polarization. The inference in C8 is reasonable given the data, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: BMDMs from immunotumoroids containing MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells show increased surface expression of M1-like markers (MHCII, CD86) and decreased expression of M2-like markers (CD163, CD206).
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 are supported by flow cytometry data from 3D immunotumoroid cultures (Figure 2B-C). The results are consistent with the transcriptomic data (C7) and provide protein-level validation. Statistical significance is demonstrated with n=5 independent experiments, providing adequate replication.

results.result: MPS1i-treated cancer cells show decreased anti-Tyrp1 antibody binding and are approximately 20% larger in size as measured by flow cytometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C). The increased cell size is consistent with known effects of CIN including cytokinesis defects and polyploidy. The decreased Tyrp1 binding is an important observation for interpreting subsequent phagocytosis experiments, though the mechanism is not explored.

results.result: CIN-afflicted tumoroids are eliminated by BMDMs regardless of anti-Tyrp1 opsonization, whereas anti-Tyrp1 is required for clearance of DMSO control tumoroids.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by 3D tumoroid phagocytosis assays (Figure 2D-E). The data show clear differential responses based on CIN status and opsonization. The results are consistent across multiple timepoints and provide functional validation of the M1 polarization observed in earlier claims. Sample size appears adequate (n=16 tumoroids from 2 experiments).

results.result: CIN-afflicted tumors show substantially increased immune infiltration at day 5 post-challenge, including 3-fold more CD45+ immune cells, 2.5-fold more myeloid cells, 6-fold more F4/80+ macrophages, and 6-fold more M1-like (CD86hi CD206lo) macrophages compared to controls, with M1-like macrophages outnumbering M2-like by 2-fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 are supported by flow cytometry analysis of tumor infiltrates (Figure 2G). The data show consistent increases across multiple immune cell populations with adequate sample sizes (n=5-8 mice). The findings align with earlier in vitro observations and provide in vivo validation. Statistical significance is demonstrated for all comparisons.

results.result: Mice challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 cells (both sgCtrl and CD47 KO) show exponential tumor growth and no long-term survivors regardless of anti-Tyrp1 treatment, while CIN-afflicted sgCtrl tumors show increased median survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by in vivo tumor growth data (Figure 3B-C). The results establish important baseline controls and demonstrate that neither CD47 KO alone nor anti-Tyrp1 alone is sufficient for tumor rejection in this model. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-11 mice per group across multiple experiments). The findings are consistent with cited previous studies.

results.result: CIN-afflicted CD47 KO tumors show dramatically improved outcomes: 28% complete cures without anti-Tyrp1, 97% survival with anti-Tyrp1, and >80% survival even at the lowest MPS1i concentration tested when combined with anti-Tyrp1.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by in vivo survival data (Figure 3C-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The 97% survival rate is remarkably high and represents a major finding. The dose-response data (C25) strengthen the conclusion by showing efficacy even at low CIN levels. Sample sizes are substantial (n=14-35 mice depending on condition across multiple experiments), providing strong statistical power.

results.result: Adoptive transfer of engineered bone marrow enables survival of mice with CIN-afflicted WT tumors: 37% with anti-SIRPα blockade, 50% with anti-Tyrp1 priming, and 80% with both combined.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by adoptive transfer experiments (Figure 3E). The data demonstrate that macrophages are key effector cells and that both CD47-SIRPα disruption and IgG opsonization contribute to efficacy. The synergistic effect of combining both approaches (80% survival) is particularly notable. Sample sizes appear adequate though exact numbers per group are not specified in the claims.

results.result: Convalescent sera from survivors contain significantly elevated levels of IgG2a/c and IgG2b antibodies that bind both Tyrp1-positive and Tyrp1 KO B16F10 cells, indicating recognition of multiple tumor antigens beyond Tyrp1.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by flow cytometry and western blotting data (Figure 4B). The binding to Tyrp1 KO cells provides strong evidence for epitope spreading. Sample sizes are substantial (n=14-28 sera samples). The western blot qualitatively confirms multiple bands, supporting multi-epitope recognition. Statistical significance is demonstrated using appropriate non-parametric tests.

results.result: Convalescent sera promote phagocytosis of CD47 KO B16F10 cells at levels comparable to anti-Tyrp1 (~5-fold increase), and continue to enhance phagocytosis even in CD47/Tyrp1 double KO cells (~3-fold increase).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 are supported by 2D phagocytosis assays (Figure 4C-i). The functional validation of IgG activity is important for demonstrating biological relevance. The persistence of activity against double KO cells confirms targeting of antigens beyond Tyrp1. Sample sizes are large (n=14-23 sera samples), providing robust statistics.

results.result: Convalescent serum IgG suppresses growth of B16F10 CD47 KO tumoroids in vitro and achieves tumor elimination in vivo with cure rates (25%) nearly identical to anti-Tyrp1 (22%) when used for pre-opsonization.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by 3D tumoroid assays and in vivo pre-opsonization experiments (Figure 4C-ii, 4D). The comparable efficacy to anti-Tyrp1 monoclonal antibody is notable given that sera contain polyclonal antibodies. The in vivo validation strengthens the conclusion, though cure rates are modest compared to the 97% achieved with fresh anti-Tyrp1 treatment (C24).

results.result: Re-challenge experiments show that survivors have limited protection against DMSO-treated tumors (9% survival, but increased median survival from 14 to 21 days), but complete protection (100% survival) against MPS1i-treated tumors, even without anti-Tyrp1.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 are supported by second challenge survival data (Figure 4F). The differential response to CIN-afflicted versus stable tumors is striking and suggests that ongoing CIN provides antigens that maintain immune responses. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-11 mice per group). The results are consistent with the IgG data and provide functional validation of acquired immunity.

results.result: Non-surviving mice from second challenge show enhanced immune infiltration compared to naïve mice, including 2-fold increases in total immune cells and CD8+ T cells, 3-fold increase in macrophages, and 4-fold increase in MHCII-high M1-like macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 are supported by flow cytometry analysis of second challenge tumors (Figure 4G). The data demonstrate enhanced cell-mediated immunity even in non-survivors, suggesting partial immune memory. Sample sizes are small (n=3-5 mice) but statistical significance is achieved. The findings provide mechanistic insight into the improved median survival observed in C38.

results.result: In a third tumor challenge, approximately 56% of long-term survivors completely resist tumor growth when challenged with untreated B16F10 CD47 KO cells without any therapeutic intervention.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by third challenge survival data (Figure 4H-i). The high rate of complete resistance demonstrates durable acquired immunity. The sample size is reasonable (n=9 mice) though relatively small. The result represents a strong validation of the vaccination-like effect of CIN-afflicted tumor clearance.

results.result: Comparison of tumor growth in T- and B-cell deficient NSG mice versus immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice shows similar growth delays with MPS1i treatment, indicating that macrophages rather than T and B cells are the key initiating-effector cells in rejecting CIN-afflicted tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by comparative studies in NSG and C57BL/6 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and adoptive transfer experiments. The similar growth delays in both mouse strains provide strong evidence that T and B cells are not required for initial tumor control. However, the inference in C47 that macrophages are the key initiating effectors, while well-supported by the adoptive transfer data (C26-C28), could benefit from additional depletion experiments.

results.result: A 97% survival rate is achieved in immunocompetent mice challenged with CIN-afflicted B16F10 tumors when maximizing macrophage-mediated activity through CD47 disruption and IgG opsonization, demonstrating that early-stage CIN generates anti-cancer vulnerabilities favoring macrophage-mediated immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 synthesize the major finding of the study, supported by the in vivo survival data (Figure 3C-D). The 97% survival rate is exceptionally high for this poorly immunogenic tumor model. The conclusion that CIN generates vulnerabilities is well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches. This represents the central thesis of the manuscript.

results.result: Survivors develop de novo anti-cancer IgG that are pro-phagocytic, multi-epitope, and efficacious in vivo. Early-stage CIN facilitates survival while generating IgGs that drive positive phagocytic feedback, and ongoing CIN strengthens cell-mediated immunity while creating an antigen reservoir for long-term humoral immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 synthesize findings from the IgG characterization and re-challenge experiments. The claims are well-supported by data showing IgG generation (C29-C31), functional activity (C32-C36), and improved responses in re-challenges (C37-C44). The mechanistic interpretations in C51-C52 are reasonable inferences from the data, though they represent hypotheses that could benefit from additional mechanistic studies.

results.result: Prior studies have shown that highly aneuploid tumors contain M2-polarized macrophages, MPS1i-treated cells can escape immune clearance, and cancer cells respond to CIN with IL6-STAT3 signaling that protects from cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 accurately represent findings from cited literature (Davoli et al. 2017, Taylor et al. 2018, Wang et al. 2021, Hong et al. 2022). These claims provide important context for the current study by highlighting apparent contradictions with prior work. The authors appropriately distinguish between late-stage highly aneuploid tumors (prior studies) and early-stage CIN (current study).

results.result: Ploidy changes increase pro-phagocytic factors, phagocytosis is inhibited by CD47-SIRPα interaction, and maximal phagocytosis requires disruption of this checkpoint.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 represent established knowledge in the field, supported by cited literature (Chao et al. 2010, Krysko et al. 2018, Oldenborg et al. 2000, Tsai and Discher 2008). These claims provide essential background for the experimental design and interpretation. The knowledge is well-established and appropriately cited.

results.result: Clinical trials of CD47 blockade have shown limited efficacy and safety concerns, CIN inhibits tumor growth in immunocompetent but not immunocompromised mice, early-stage CIN induces senescence and inflammatory pathways, and B16F10 tumors are poorly immunogenic with modest response to macrophage-directed therapies.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 provide important clinical and experimental context. C59 accurately reflects the status of CD47-targeting clinical trials. C60-C61 are supported by cited literature (Senovilla et al. 2012, Boilève et al. 2013, Santaguida et al. 2017, Wang et al. 2021). C62 is supported by both general knowledge and cited studies (Dooling et al. 2023, Hayes et al. 2023). These contextual claims appropriately frame the significance of the current findings.

results.result: MPS1 inhibitor treatment induces chromosomal instability (CIN) in B16F10 cells, as evidenced by >10-fold increases in micronuclei that persist up to 12 days and 34% of cells showing aneuploidy by InferCNV analysis.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly accept that MPS1 inhibition leads to CIN. The first reviewer states the authors 'provide compelling evidence that MSP1 inhibition (leading to chromosomal instability or CIN in the cancer cells) increases phagocytosis,' and the second reviewer confirms 'MSP1 inhibition, most notable for causing chromosomal instability (CIN).' No concerns are raised about these foundational CIN measurements.

results.result: Tumors comprised of MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells show downregulated M2-like macrophage markers (Arg1, Marco, Cd274, Ccl2, Ccl4, Ccl7, Ccl22, Il21r) and downregulated pathways related to DNA damage, cell cycle, and growth by gene set enrichment analysis.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not question these bulk RNA-sequencing findings from whole tumors. The first reviewer notes the study demonstrates 'tumors with CIN respond better to macrophage therapeutics,' implicitly accepting the transcriptomic changes. The second reviewer does not raise concerns about these data.

results.result: BMDMs treated with conditioned media from MPS1i-treated B16F10 cells show increased M1-like anti-cancer markers and decreased M2-like pro-cancer markers, suggesting that early-stage CIN activates macrophages via secreted factors toward M1-like anti-cancer activity.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly highlights this as 'the most compelling experiment,' stating that 'transferring conditioned media from MSP1 inhibited and control cancer cells, then using RNAseq to demonstrate that the MSP1-inhibited conditioned media causes a shift towards a more tumoricidal macrophage phenotype' is particularly strong evidence. No concerns are raised about these findings.

results.result: BMDMs from immunotumoroids of MPS1i-treated B16F10 show increased M1-like markers (MHCII, CD86) and decreased M2-like markers (CD163, CD206), while MPS1i-treated cancer cells show decreased anti-Tyrp1 binding and ~20% larger size.
results.evaluation: These flow cytometry findings from 3D tumoroid systems are not questioned by reviewers. The data support the macrophage polarization findings and are consistent with the conditioned media experiments that reviewers found compelling.

results.result: CIN-afflicted tumoroids are eliminated by BMDMs regardless of anti-Tyrp1 opsonization, whereas anti-Tyrp1 is required for clearance of DMSO control tumoroids.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not challenge these phagocytosis assay results. The first reviewer notes the study demonstrates 'MSP1 inhibition...increases phagocytosis,' accepting these functional findings. The differential requirement for opsonization is not questioned.

results.result: CIN-afflicted tumors show 3-fold more CD45+ immune cells, 2.5-fold more CD11b+ myeloid cells, ~6-fold increase in F4/80+ macrophages, and approximately 6-fold more M1-like (CD86hi CD206lo) macrophages compared to DMSO controls at day 5 post-challenge.
results.evaluation: These in vivo immune infiltration data are not questioned by reviewers. The findings are consistent with the overall narrative that reviewers accept regarding increased macrophage infiltration and polarization in CIN tumors.

results.result: All mice challenged with DMSO-treated B16F10 cells (both sgCtrl and CD47 KO) show exponential tumor growth and no survivors, while CIN-afflicted sgCtrl tumors show increased median survival.
results.evaluation: These baseline control findings are not questioned by reviewers and establish the context for the therapeutic interventions. The data are consistent with cited previous studies.

results.result: CIN-afflicted CD47 KO tumors show 28% complete cures without anti-Tyrp1 and 97% survival when paired with anti-Tyrp1 treatment, with >80% survival even at the lowest MPS1i concentration causing just 10% micronuclei.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer explicitly describes these as 'particularly impressive survival rates for mouse models of CIN B16 tumors treated with adoptively transferred macrophages, CD47-SIRPα blockade, and anti-Tyrp1 IgG.' The second reviewer notes 'a combination of CD47 knockdown and anti-Tyrp1 IgG is sufficient for long term survival in nearly all mice' and calls this 'a striking improvement from conditions without CIN.'

results.result: Adoptive marrow transfer experiments show that 37% of mice survive with anti-SIRPα-blocked marrow, 50% with anti-Tyrp1-primed marrow, and 80% with combined anti-SIRPα blockade and anti-Tyrp1 priming when challenged with CIN-afflicted WT tumors.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer explicitly mentions 'adoptively transferred macrophages' as part of the impressive survival rates. These adoptive transfer experiments are not questioned and support the conclusion about macrophage importance.

results.result: Convalescent sera from survivors show significantly increased IgG2a/c and IgG2b binding against both Tyrp1-positive and Tyrp1 KO B16F10 cells, indicating antibodies target a repertoire of antigens beyond Tyrp1.
results.evaluation: These antibody response data are not questioned by reviewers. The findings support the development of adaptive immunity following CIN tumor clearance.

results.result: Convalescent sera increase phagocytosis of CD47 KO B16F10 cells by ~5-fold (identical to anti-Tyrp1), continue to promote phagocytosis in CD47/Tyrp1 double KO cells (~3-fold), and lead to tumoroid elimination or suppressed growth in 3D assays.
results.evaluation: These functional antibody data are not challenged by reviewers and demonstrate the pro-phagocytic activity of the induced antibody response.

results.result: Pre-opsonization with convalescent sera or anti-Tyrp1 yields near identical cure rates (25% and 22%). Previously cured mice show only 1/11 survival when re-challenged with DMSO-treated cells (though median survival increased to 21 vs 14 days), but 100% survival when re-challenged with MPS1i-treated cells.
results.evaluation: These re-challenge experiments are not questioned by reviewers and demonstrate differential protective immunity against CIN versus non-CIN tumors.

results.result: Previous survivors re-challenged with DMSO-treated cells show roughly 2-fold increases in immune cells and CD8+ T cells, near 3-fold increase in F4/80+ macrophages, and roughly 4-fold increase in MHCII-high (M1-like) macrophages compared to naïve counterparts.
results.evaluation: These immune memory data are not questioned by reviewers and support the development of acquired immunity following initial CIN tumor clearance.

results.result: In a third tumor challenge, ~56% of mice completely resist tumor growth when challenged with untreated B16F10 CD47 KO cells without anti-Tyrp1 treatment.
results.evaluation: This finding demonstrating progressive immune memory is not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: Similar growth delays are found for MPS1i-pre-treated B16F10 cells in T- and B-cell deficient NSG mice and immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice, leading to the conclusion that T and B cells are not key initiating-effector cells and that macrophages are the key initiating-effector cells in rejecting CIN-afflicted tumors.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not challenge these NSG versus C57BL/6 comparison data or the conclusion about macrophages being key effector cells. The second reviewer notes the study demonstrates macrophages can be 'powerful enough to permanently eliminate a tumor,' accepting the macrophage-centric interpretation.

results.result: A 97% survival rate is achieved in immunocompetent mice challenged with CIN-afflicted, syngeneic B16F10 tumors when maximizing macrophage-mediated activity, suggesting that CIN in early stages generates anti-cancer vulnerabilities that favor macrophage-mediated immune response contingent on conditions for maximal phagocytosis.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer explicitly states the authors 'demonstrate particularly impressive survival rates' and the second reviewer calls the combination therapy results 'a striking improvement.' Both reviewers accept the overall conclusion about CIN creating vulnerabilities for macrophage attack.

results.result: Survivors develop de novo anti-cancer IgG that are pro-phagocytic, multi-epitope, and efficacious in vivo. Early-stage CIN facilitates survival while generating potent IgGs that drive positive phagocytic feedback to minimize recurrence, and ongoing CIN can strengthen cell-mediated acquired immunity and create an antigen reservoir for long-term humoral immunity.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the antibody generation data, the second reviewer raises a critical caveat: 'chromosomal instability is driven by MSP1 inhibition in all the experiments, leaving open the possibility that some effects are due to MSP1 inhibition specifically rather than CIN more generally.' This uncertainty about mechanism attribution affects the broader mechanistic conclusions about CIN's role in immunity.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on C1-C3. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers accept that MPS1 inhibition successfully induces CIN, with converging evidence from multiple assays. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Agreement on C4-C6. Both accept the bulk RNA-sequencing findings from whole tumors. OpenEval notes the limitation of n=2 tumors per condition, while peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these data.

Strong agreement on C7-C8. Both evaluations support the conditioned media experiment showing M1 polarization. Peer reviewers explicitly highlight this as 'the most compelling experiment,' while OpenEval finds the clustering analysis and marker expression patterns convincing.
Agreement on C9-C10. Both accept the flow cytometry validation of M1 polarization in 3D tumoroids. Peer review R4 also covers C11-C12, which OpenEval addresses separately in R5.
Agreement on C11-C12. Both accept the cell size increase and decreased Tyrp1 binding findings. Peer review groups these with C9-C10 in a single result, while OpenEval separates them.
Agreement on C13-C14. Both accept the 3D tumoroid phagocytosis assay results showing differential responses based on CIN status and opsonization. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Agreement on C15-C19. Both accept the in vivo immune infiltration data showing increased macrophages and other immune cells. Findings are consistent with the overall narrative accepted by both evaluations.
Agreement on C20-C22. Both accept the baseline control findings establishing that neither CD47 KO alone nor anti-Tyrp1 alone is sufficient for tumor rejection. No concerns raised.

Strong agreement on C23-C25. Both evaluations explicitly highlight the impressive 97% survival rate with combination therapy. Peer reviewers call this 'a striking improvement,' while OpenEval notes the remarkably high survival rate and substantial sample sizes.

Agreement on C26-C28. Both accept the adoptive transfer experiments demonstrating macrophages as key effector cells. Peer reviewers explicitly mention adoptively transferred macrophages as part of impressive survival rates.
Agreement on C29-C31. Both accept the antibody response data showing IgG generation and epitope spreading. No concerns raised about these findings.
Agreement on C32-C34. Both accept the functional validation of IgG pro-phagocytic activity. Peer review R11 also covers C35, which OpenEval addresses in R13.
Agreement on C35. Both accept the comparable efficacy of sera to anti-Tyrp1 monoclonal antibody in 3D tumoroids. OpenEval also addresses C36 in this result, which peer review covers in R12.
Agreement on C36. Both accept the in vivo pre-opsonization experiments. Peer review R12 also covers C37-C39, which OpenEval addresses separately in R14.
Agreement on C37-C39. Both accept the second challenge survival data showing differential protective immunity against CIN versus non-CIN tumors. No concerns raised.
Agreement on C40-C43. Both accept the immune memory data from second challenge tumors showing enhanced cell-mediated immunity. No concerns raised about these findings.
Agreement on C44. Both accept the third challenge survival data demonstrating durable acquired immunity. No concerns raised.

Agreement on C45-C47. Both accept the NSG versus C57BL/6 comparison data and the conclusion about macrophages being key effector cells. OpenEval suggests additional depletion experiments would strengthen C47, while peer reviewers do not raise this concern.

Strong agreement on C48-C49. Both evaluations explicitly praise the impressive survival rates and accept the overall conclusion about CIN creating vulnerabilities for macrophage attack. This represents the central thesis accepted by both.

Partial disagreement on C50-C52. OpenEval finds these mechanistic synthesis claims well-supported, noting they represent reasonable inferences that could benefit from additional studies. Peer reviewers rate this as UNCERTAIN, raising a critical caveat that effects may be due to MSP1 inhibition specifically rather than CIN more generally, affecting mechanism attribution.

OpenEval evaluates C53-C55 (literature context about CIN and immune evasion) as supported, noting these claims appropriately distinguish between late-stage highly aneuploid tumors and early-stage CIN. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates C56-C58 (established background on calreticulin, CD47, and 'don't eat me' signals) as supported with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates C59-C62 (clinical and experimental context including CD47-targeting trials and CIN effects) as supported with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
